p.src: Now Gongsun Yuan was the grandson of Gongsun Du of Liaodong and the son of Gongsun Kang. In the twelfth year of Jian'an, Cao Cao pursued Yuan Shang. Before he reached Liaodong, Gongsun Kang beheaded Yuan Shang and presented his head to Cao Cao, who enfeoffed Kang as Marquis of Xiangping. After Kang died, he left two sons, the elder named Huang and the younger Yuan, but both were still children. Kang's younger brother, Gongsun Gong, therefore succeeded to his office. In Cao Pi's reign, Gong was appointed General of Chariots and Cavalry and Marquis of Xiangping. In the second year of Taihe, Yuan came of age. Accomplished in both civil and military affairs, he was headstrong and fond of conflict. He seized the position of his uncle Gongsun Gong, whereupon Cao Rui appointed him General Who Displays Martial Might and Administrator of Liaodong. Later, Sun Quan sent Zhang Mi and Xu Yan to Liaodong bearing gold, treasures, and precious jade, and conferred upon Yuan the title King of Yan. Fearing the power of the Central Plains, Yuan beheaded both Zhang and Xu and sent their heads to Cao Rui. Cao Rui appointed Yuan Grand Marshal and Duke of Lelang. Still unsatisfied, Yuan consulted his followers, proclaimed himself King of Yan, and inaugurated the first year of the Shaohan era. His deputy Jia Fan remonstrated: “The Central Plains has treated you, my lord, with the rank of one of the highest nobles; that is no low or contemptible station. If you now rebel against them, it would truly be an act of disloyalty. Moreover, Sima Yi is highly skilled in warfare. Even Marquis Zhuge of Western Shu could not defeat him—how then could you, my lord?”

p.src: Yuan flew into a rage and ordered his attendants to bind Jia Fan and take him away for execution. The staff officer Lun Zhi remonstrated: “Jia Fan speaks the truth. The sage said, ‘When a state is about to perish, portents of evil are sure to appear.’ Strange occurrences have lately appeared time and again throughout our land. Recently a dog was seen wearing a kerchief and cap and dressed in red, walking upright like a man upon a rooftop. Again, when villagers south of the city were cooking rice, a small child suddenly appeared inside the steamer, boiled to death. And in Xiangping's northern market, the ground suddenly collapsed into a pit, from which emerged a mass of flesh several feet around. It possessed a head and face, eyes, ears, mouth, and nose, but no hands or feet. Neither blades nor arrows could wound it, and no one knew what it was. A diviner interpreted it thus: ‘It has form but is not complete; it has a mouth but makes no sound. Because the state is destined for destruction, it has revealed this form.’ These three occurrences are all inauspicious omens. You should avoid calamity and seek good fortune, my lord, and must not act rashly.” Yuan erupted in fury. He ordered his guards to bind Lun Zhi and behead him in the marketplace together with Jia Fan. Then he appointed the Great General Bei Yan as commander and Yang Zuo as vanguard, raised one hundred and fifty thousand troops from Liaodong, and drove toward the Central Plains.

p.src: The frontier officials reported the news to Cao Rui, ruler of Wei. Greatly alarmed, Rui summoned Sima Yi to court for consultation. Yi memorialized: “The forty thousand cavalry and infantry under my command will be sufficient to destroy the rebels.” Rui said, “Your troops are few and the road is long. I fear recovery of the region will be difficult.” Yi replied, “Victory does not depend upon numbers, but upon devising surprises and employing wisdom. Relying upon Your Majesty's abundant fortune, I shall surely capture Gongsun Yuan and present him before you.” Rui asked, “What action do you expect Gongsun Yuan to take?” Yi replied, “If Yuan abandons his city and flees beforehand, that will be his best plan. If he defends Liaodong against the imperial army, that will be his middle plan. If he merely shuts himself inside Xiangping, that will be his worst plan, and he will certainly be captured by me.” Rui asked, “How long will the journey there and back require?” Yi replied, “The distance is four thousand li: one hundred days to go, one hundred days to attack, and sixty days to rest. About one year will suffice.” Rui said, “What if Wu or Shu invades?” Yi replied, “I have already established plans for the defense. Your Majesty need not worry.” Rui was delighted and at once ordered Sima Yi to raise an army and punish Gongsun Yuan. Yi took leave of the court and departed the capital. He appointed Hu Zun as vanguard and sent him ahead with the leading division to encamp in Liaodong. A mounted scout sped to inform Gongsun Yuan. Yuan ordered Bei Yan and Yang Zuo to divide eighty thousand troops and station them at Liaosui. Their encircling trenches extended more than twenty li and were ringed with abatis, making the defenses exceedingly secure. Hu Zun sent word of this to Sima Yi. Yi laughed and said, “The rebels refuse to fight because they mean to wear down our army. I judge that more than half their forces are here, leaving their lair undefended. We would do better to abandon this place and advance directly upon Xiangping. The rebels will surely hasten to its rescue. We shall strike them on the road and achieve complete victory.” He therefore mustered his troops and advanced along byways toward Xiangping.

p.src: Meanwhile, Bei Yan and Yang Zuo were consulting together. “If the Wei army attacks, we must not engage it. They have come a thousand li, and their supplies cannot be maintained. They will find it difficult to hold out, and when their provisions are exhausted, they must retreat. When they withdraw, we shall strike with a surprise force, and Sima Yi can be captured. Formerly, when Sima Yi resisted the army of Shu, he held firm south of the Wei River until Kongming finally died in camp. The same principle applies today.” While the two were still discussing this, a sudden report came: “The Wei army has gone south.” Bei Yan was greatly alarmed. “They know that Xiangping is lightly defended and have gone to raid our main base. If Xiangping falls, there will be no purpose in our holding this place.” They therefore struck camp and set out in pursuit. A scout had already sped ahead to report this to Sima Yi. Yi laughed. “They have fallen into my trap!” He ordered Xiahou Ba and Xiahou Wei each to lead a force into ambush on the banks of the Ji River: “When the Liaodong troops arrive, attack together from both sides.” The two received the plan and departed. Before long they saw Bei Yan and Yang Zuo approaching at the head of their troops. At the blast of a cannon, drums thundered and banners waved on both sides. Xiahou Ba charged from the left and Xiahou Wei from the right, both attacking at once. Bei and Yang had no heart for battle and fled, forcing a path through the enemy. Reaching Mount Shou, they encountered Gongsun Yuan's approaching army. They joined forces, turned their horses, and again engaged the Wei troops. Bei Yan rode forth and cursed: “Rebel general, cease your treacherous schemes! Do you dare come out and fight?” Xiahou Ba spurred forward, brandishing his saber to meet him. Within only a few bouts, Xiahou Ba struck Bei Yan from his horse with a single stroke, and the Liaodong army fell into chaos. Ba drove his troops forward in pursuit. Gongsun Yuan led the defeated soldiers into Xiangping, closed the gates, and held fast without emerging. The Wei army closed in around the city on all four sides.

p.src: It was then the season of autumn rains. They fell without cease for a month, until the water stood three feet deep upon the level ground and grain ships could sail directly from the mouth of the Liao River to the walls of Xiangping. The Wei troops were all standing in water and could neither move nor rest in comfort. Pei Jing, Commander of the Left, entered the command tent and reported: “The rain will not stop, and the camp is deep in mud. The army cannot remain here. I ask that we move to the mountain ahead.” Yi said angrily, “Gongsun Yuan will be captured within days. How can we move camp? Anyone who speaks again of moving camp will be beheaded!” Pei Jing murmured his assent and withdrew. A short while later, Qiu Lian, Commander of the Right, also came to report: “The soldiers are suffering from the floodwaters. I beg the Grand Commandant to move camp to higher ground.” Yi flew into a rage. “My military order has already been issued. How dare you deliberately defy it!” He immediately ordered Qiu Lian dragged out and beheaded, and had his head hung outside the southern gate. The whole army was thereby struck with awe.

p.src: Yi ordered the troops in two camps to withdraw temporarily twenty li, allowing the soldiers and people within the city to come out to cut firewood and pasture their cattle and horses. The army secretary Chen Qun asked: “When Your Excellency formerly attacked Shangyong, you divided the army into eight columns, hastened to the walls in eight days, and achieved the great feat of capturing Meng Da alive. Now you have brought forty thousand armored troops several thousand li, yet you do not order an assault upon the city. Instead, you keep them long amid the mud and even allow the rebels to gather firewood and graze their animals. I truly cannot understand Your Excellency's intention.” Yi laughed. “Do you not understand the art of war? Formerly, Meng Da had abundant provisions but few troops, while I had little grain but many troops; therefore, I had no choice but to seek a swift battle. Only by taking him unawares and attacking suddenly could I prevail. Now the Liaodong troops are many and ours are few, while the enemy is hungry and we are well fed. Why should we storm the city by force? We should let them flee of their own accord, then seize the opportunity to strike. By leaving an escape route open and not preventing them from gathering wood and pasturing their animals, I am giving them the opportunity to flee.” Chen Qun bowed in admiration.

p.src: The generals received their orders. At first light the next day, they led their troops to close in from all four sides, raised earthen mounds, dug tunnels, erected artillery frames, and set up scaling ladders. They attacked without respite day and night, while arrows poured into the city like driving rain. Inside the city Gongsun Yuan’s provisions were exhausted, and cattle and horses were slaughtered for food. Everyone was bitterly resentful and had lost the will to defend the city; they wished to behead Yuan, offer up the city, and surrender. Hearing this, Yuan grew deeply alarmed and anxious. In haste he ordered his Chancellor of State, Wang Jian, and his Censor-in-Chief, Liu Fu, to go to the Wei camp and ask to surrender. The two were lowered by ropes from the city wall. They came before Sima Yi and said, “We ask the Grand Commandant to withdraw twenty li; then our lord and his ministers will come in person to surrender.” Sima Yi flew into a rage and said, “Why does Gongsun Yuan not come himself? This is utterly unreasonable!” He shouted for the guards to drag them out and behead them, then gave their heads to their attendants.

p.src: When the attendants returned with their report, Gongsun Yuan was greatly alarmed and sent Palace Attendant Wei Yan to the Wei camp. Sima Yi took his seat in the command tent and assembled his generals in ranks on either side. Wei Yan advanced on his knees, knelt below the tent, and said, “May the Grand Commandant calm his thunderous wrath. On an appointed day we shall first send the heir, Gongsun Xiu, as a hostage. Afterward, our lord and his ministers will come bound to surrender.” Sima Yi said, “There are five essential courses in warfare: if one can fight, one should fight; if one cannot fight, one should defend; if one cannot defend, one should flee; if one cannot flee, one should surrender; and if one cannot surrender, one should die. What need is there to send a son as hostage?” He angrily ordered Wei Yan to return and report this to Gongsun Yuan. Wei Yan fled away in abject terror and returned to inform Gongsun Yuan. Yuan was greatly alarmed. After secretly settling a plan with his son Gongsun Xiu, he selected a thousand soldiers and horsemen. During the second watch that night, they opened the south gate and fled southeast. Seeing no one about, Yuan rejoiced inwardly. Before they had gone ten li, a cannon suddenly sounded from the hills, drums and horns blared together, and a force barred their way. At its center was Sima Yi; Sima Shi was on the left and Sima Zhao on the right. The two shouted, “Rebels, do not flee!” Yuan was terrified and hastily wheeled his horse about to seek another road of escape. But Hu Zun’s troops had already arrived; Xiahou Ba and Xiahou Wei were on the left, Zhang Hu and Yue Chen on the right; they enclosed them on all sides as tightly as an iron barrel. Gongsun Yuan and his son had no choice but to dismount and submit. Still on horseback, Sima Yi looked round at his generals and said, “On the bingyin night five days ago, I saw the great star fall here. Tonight, the renshen day, the omen has been fulfilled.” The generals offered their congratulations, saying, “The Grand Commandant’s divine foresight is truly wondrous!” Sima Yi gave the order to behead them. Gongsun Yuan and his son were executed before each other’s eyes. Sima Yi then marshaled his army and advanced to take Xiangping. Before he reached the city walls, Hu Zun had already led his troops inside. The people burned incense and bowed in welcome. All the Wei troops entered the city. Sima Yi took his seat in the government hall and put to death Gongsun Yuan’s clansmen, together with the officials and others who had conspired with him; more than seventy heads were counted. He posted proclamations to reassure the people. Someone informed Sima Yi, “Jia Fan and Lun Zhi earnestly remonstrated with Yuan against rebelling, and both were killed by him.” Sima Yi therefore honored their graves and bestowed distinction upon their descendants; then he distributed the treasure in the storehouses to reward the three armies and led his forces back to Luoyang.

p.src: Now the Ruler of Wei was in his palace when, at the third watch of the night, a sudden cold, uncanny wind extinguished the lamps. He saw Empress Mao leading several dozen palace women, weeping as they approached his seat and demanded his life. Rui fell ill from this encounter. As his illness steadily worsened, he ordered the Palace Attendants and Grand Masters for Splendid Happiness Liu Fang and Sun Zi to manage all affairs of the Privy Council; he also summoned Cao Yu, Prince of Yan and a son of Emperor Wen, appointing him General-in-Chief to assist the crown prince Cao Fang as regent. Cao Yu was respectful, frugal, mild, and peaceable. Unwilling to bear so great a responsibility, he firmly declined the appointment. Rui summoned Liu Fang and Sun Zi and asked, “Who among the imperial clan is fit for the post?” The two had long been indebted to Cao Zhen, so they recommended, “Only Cao Shuang, son of Cao Zidan, is suitable.” Rui accepted their advice. The two further memorialized, “If Your Majesty wishes to employ Cao Shuang, the Prince of Yan must be sent back to his fief.” Rui approved their words. The two then asked Rui to issue an edict, which they carried out and proclaimed to the Prince of Yan: “Here is the Emperor’s handwritten edict, commanding the Prince of Yan to return to his fief and depart this very day; without an edict, you are forbidden to enter the court.” The Prince of Yan departed in tears. Cao Shuang was then appointed General-in-Chief and placed in overall charge of the government.

u.src: Now the Ruler of Wei was in his palace when, at the third watch of the night, a sudden cold, uncanny wind extinguished the lamps.
He saw Empress Mao leading several dozen palace women, weeping as they approached his seat and demanded his life. Rui fell ill from this encounter.
As his illness steadily worsened, he ordered the Palace Attendants and Grand Masters for Splendid Happiness Liu Fang and Sun Zi to manage all affairs of the Privy Council;
he also summoned Cao Yu, Prince of Yan and a son of Emperor Wen, appointing him General-in-Chief to assist the crown prince Cao Fang as regent.
Cao Yu was respectful, frugal, mild, and peaceable. Unwilling to bear so great a responsibility, he firmly declined the appointment.
Rui summoned Liu Fang and Sun Zi and asked, “Who among the imperial clan is fit for the post?”
The two had long been indebted to Cao Zhen, so they recommended, “Only Cao Shuang, son of Cao Zidan, is suitable.”
Rui accepted their advice.
The two further memorialized, “If Your Majesty wishes to employ Cao Shuang, the Prince of Yan must be sent back to his fief.”
Rui approved their words.

The two then asked Rui to issue an edict, which they carried out and proclaimed to the Prince of Yan: “Here is the Emperor’s handwritten edict, commanding the Prince of Yan to return to his fief and depart this very day;
without an edict, you are forbidden to enter the court.”
The Prince of Yan departed in tears.
Cao Shuang was then appointed General-in-Chief and placed in overall charge of the government.

p.src: As Rui’s condition grew critical, he urgently sent an envoy bearing the imperial tally and an edict recalling Sima Yi to court. Receiving the command, Sima Yi went directly to Xuchang and entered the palace to see the Ruler of Wei. Rui said, “I feared only that I would not live to see you; now that I have seen you today, I can die without regret.” Sima Yi bowed his head to the ground and memorialized, “On the road I heard that Your Majesty’s sacred person was unwell, and I bitterly regretted that no two wings grew from my ribs to carry me flying to the palace gates. That I behold Your Majesty’s countenance today is my great fortune.” Rui summoned the crown prince Cao Fang, General-in-Chief Cao Shuang, the Palace Attendants Liu Fang and Sun Zi, and the others, and had them all come before the imperial couch. Taking Sima Yi by the hand, Rui said, “Long ago, when Liu Xuande lay gravely ill at Baidi Castle, he entrusted his young son Liu Shan to Zhuge Kongming. Kongming thereafter devoted his utmost loyalty to the task and did not rest until death. If such a thing could be done in a minor state, how much more so in a great realm? My young son Cao Fang is only eight years old and is not capable of governing the realm. I trust that you, Grand Commandant, together with my kinsman and the veteran ministers of merit, will exert all your strength to assist him and not betray my hopes!” Then he called Cao Fang and said, “Zhongda and I are as one; you must honor and respect him.” He then ordered Sima Yi to bring Cao Fang nearer. Cao Fang threw his arms around Sima Yi’s neck and would not let go. Rui said, “Grand Commandant, do not forget the affection my young son has shown you today!” When he had finished speaking, tears streamed down his face. Sima Yi bowed his head to the ground and wept. The Ruler of Wei sank into a stupor and could no longer speak. He merely pointed at the crown prince, and a short while later he died; he had reigned for thirteen years and lived to the age of thirty-six. It was late in the first month of spring, in the third year of Wei’s Jingchu era.

p.src: Sima Yi and Cao Shuang then supported the Crown Prince Cao Fang in ascending the imperial throne. Fang, whose courtesy name was Lanqing, was an adopted son whom Rui had taken in. He had been kept secretly within the palace, and no one knew where he had come from. Cao Fang now gave Rui the posthumous title Emperor Ming and buried him at Gaoping陵. He honored Empress Guo as Empress Dowager; and changed the era name, inaugurating the first year of Zhengshi. Sima Yi and Cao Shuang served as regents. Shuang treated Yi with the utmost deference and always informed him before deciding any important matter. Shuang's courtesy name was Zhaobo, and from childhood he had frequented the palace; Emperor Ming found him prudent and held him in great affection and esteem. Among the five hundred retainers at Shuang's gate were five men who vied with one another in fashionable affectation. The first was He Yan, courtesy name Pingshu; another was Deng Yang, courtesy name Xuanmao, a descendant of Deng Yu; another was Li Sheng, courtesy name Gongzhao; another was Ding Mi, courtesy name Yanjing; and another was Bi Gui, courtesy name Zhaoxian. There was also Huan Fan, Minister of Agriculture, courtesy name Yuanze, a man of considerable resourcefulness whom many called the “Wise Pouch.” All these men enjoyed Shuang's confidence. He Yan told Shuang, “My lord, supreme authority must not be entrusted to another, lest it bring future trouble.” Shuang replied, “Lord Sima and I both received the late emperor's charge to protect his orphan. How could I bear to betray it?” Yan said, “When your late father and Zhongda defeated the Shu army, he repeatedly suffered this man's humiliations, and that brought about his death. Why do you not perceive it, my lord?” Shuang suddenly understood. After settling a plan with the assembled officials, he entered court and memorialized the Wei emperor Cao Fang: “Sima Yi's achievements are lofty and his virtue weighty; he should be promoted to Grand Tutor.” Fang consented, and from then on all military authority passed into Shuang's hands.

p.src: Shuang appointed his younger brother Cao Xi Central Army Commander, Cao Xun General of the Martial Guard, and Cao Yan Palace Attendant. Each commanded three thousand imperial guards and was free to enter and leave the inner palace; he also made He Yan, Deng Yang, and Ding Mi Masters of Writing, Bi Gui Colonel-Director of Retainers, and Li Sheng Governor of Henan. These five deliberated with Cao Shuang day and night. Thus the number of guests at Cao Shuang's gate grew daily. Sima Yi pleaded illness and ceased appearing at court, while both his sons resigned their offices and lived in retirement. Every day Shuang drank and made merry with He Yan and the others. His garments, utensils, and vessels were in every respect indistinguishable from those of the imperial court; of every rare curiosity and plaything offered as tribute from the provinces, he first took the finest for himself and only then sent the rest into the palace. His residence and courtyards were filled with beautiful women. Zhang Dang, a palace eunuch who fawned upon Cao Shuang, secretly selected seven or eight of the late emperor's concubines and sent them to Shuang's residence. Shuang also chose thirty or forty daughters of respectable families skilled in song and dance to form his household troupe; and he built tiered towers and painted pavilions and fashioned vessels of gold and silver, employing hundreds of skilled craftsmen who labored day and night.

p.src: Now He Yan heard that Guan Lu of Pingyuan was versed in divination and invited him to discuss the Book of Changes. Deng Yang was present and asked Lu, “You claim to understand the Changes, yet your speech never touches upon its phrases or meanings. Why is that?” Lu replied, “One who truly understands the Changes does not speak of the Changes.” Yan laughed and praised him: “That may indeed be called saying the essential without needless words.” Then he said to Lu, “Cast a hexagram for me and see whether I shall attain the rank of one of the Three Excellencies.” He also asked, “For several nights I have dreamed that dozens of bluebottles gathered upon my nose. What omen is this?” Lu replied, “Yuan and Kai assisted Shun, and the Duke of Zhou aided the Zhou dynasty; through harmony, benevolence, humility, and courtesy, they enjoyed abundant blessings. Today your position is exalted and your power great, yet few cherish your virtue and many fear your might. This is hardly the way to seek blessings through circumspection. Moreover, the nose represents a mountain; a mountain remains long in honor because, though high, it is not perilous. But now foul and loathsome flies gather there. Those in lofty stations topple—how can you not be afraid? I pray that you reduce what is excessive and add to what is wanting, and never tread where propriety forbids; only then may you attain the Three Excellencies and drive away the bluebottles.” Deng Yang angrily exclaimed, “This is nothing but the usual talk of a pedantic old scholar!” Lu replied, “An old scholar sees what will not live; commonplace talk sees what will not be spoken.” With that, he shook out his sleeves and departed. The two men laughed loudly. “A true madman!” they said. When Lu reached home, he told his uncle what had happened. His uncle was greatly alarmed. “He and Deng wield enormous power. How could you offend them?” Lu replied, “I was speaking with dead men. What was there to fear?” His uncle asked the reason. Lu said, “When Deng Yang walks, his sinews do not bind his bones and his pulses do not govern his flesh. When he rises, he sways and leans as though he had neither hands nor feet. These are the signs of ‘ghostly agitation.’ As for He Yan's appearance, his soul does not remain in its dwelling, his blood lends no color to his face, and his vital spirit drifts like smoke; his countenance resembles withered wood. These are the signs of ‘ghostly seclusion.’ Sooner or later both men are certain to meet a calamity that will cost them their lives. Why should I fear them?” His uncle merely cursed Lu as a mad fellow and went away.

p.src: Now Cao Shuang often went hunting with He Yan, Deng Yang, and the others. His younger brother Cao Xi remonstrated: “Brother, your authority is too great, yet you delight in going out to hunt. Should someone plot against you, regret would come too late.” Shuang rebuked him: “Military power lies in my hands. What have I to fear?” Huan Fan, the Minister of Agriculture, also remonstrated, but Shuang would not listen. At that time the Wei emperor Cao Fang changed the tenth year of Zhengshi to the first year of Jiaping. Cao Shuang had long monopolized power but did not know Zhongda's true condition. Just then the Wei emperor appointed Li Sheng Inspector of Jingzhou. Shuang ordered Sheng to bid Zhongda farewell and use the visit to learn the truth. Sheng went straight to the Grand Tutor's residence, and a gate official promptly announced him. Sima Yi told his two sons, “Cao Shuang has sent this man to discover whether my illness is genuine.” He removed his cap, loosened his hair, climbed into bed, and sat wrapped in a quilt; then, supported by two maidservants with a staff, he had Li Sheng admitted. Sheng came before the bed, bowed, and said, “I have not seen Your Excellency for some time; who would have imagined your illness had grown so grave? Today the Son of Heaven has appointed me Inspector of Jingzhou, so I have come especially to take my leave.” Yi pretended to reply, “Bingzhou is close to the northern frontier. Make good preparations there.” Sheng said, “I have been appointed Inspector of Jingzhou, not Bingzhou.” Yi smiled. “Have you just come from Bingzhou?” Sheng replied, “Only from Qingzhou, east of the mountains.” Yi laughed loudly. “So you have come from Qingzhou.” Sheng said, “How has Your Excellency fallen so gravely ill?” The attendants said, “The Grand Tutor is deaf.” Sheng said, “Please lend me paper and brush.” The attendants brought him paper and brush. When Sheng had finished writing, he presented it. Yi read it and smiled. “My illness has truly made me deaf. Take good care of yourself on your journey.” Having spoken, he pointed to his mouth. A maid brought broth. Yi bent his mouth toward it, spilling the broth all over his lapels, then made a choking sound and said, “I am now old and mortally ill; death may come morning or evening. My two sons are unworthy; I hope you will instruct them. If you see the General-in-Chief, I beg you to ask him to look after them!” With that, he collapsed upon the bed, his voice hoarse and his breath gasping. Li Sheng took his leave of Zhongda, returned to Cao Shuang, and recounted everything in detail. Shuang was overjoyed. “If this old man dies, I shall have nothing to worry about!”

p.src: When Sima Yi saw that Li Sheng had gone, he rose and told his two sons, “Li Sheng will now report what he has seen, and Cao Shuang will surely cease to guard against me. We need only wait until he leaves the city to hunt; then we may move against him.” Before many days had passed, Cao Shuang invited the Wei emperor Cao Fang to visit Gaoping陵 and offer sacrifices to the late emperor. Officials great and small all followed the imperial carriage out of the city. Shuang, accompanied by his three younger brothers, his confidants including He Yan, and the imperial guards, was escorting the emperor onward when Huan Fan, the Minister of Agriculture, seized his horse's bridle and remonstrated: “My lord, you command all the palace troops; it is unwise for all the brothers to leave together. If some upheaval occurs within the city, what will you do?” Shuang pointed his whip at him and shouted, “Who would dare rebel? Speak no more such nonsense!” That day, when Sima Yi saw that Shuang had left the city, he rejoiced inwardly. He immediately summoned the men who had formerly served under him in defeating the enemy, together with several dozen household retainers, mounted with his two sons, and went straight out to plot Cao Shuang's destruction.
